doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Childhood car lot assault and watching September 11 from Manhattan
summary: At six a white man kicked him out of a car and his father handled it calmly; he then describes seeing the Twin Towers burn and finding his brother covered in ash.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: They were just being very outspoken about what they knew that the community needed to do and the kind of racist barriers that were being placed on us. And they were crying out and they wanted to see something — they didn’t pick up guns just to be some kind of warring militia group. They knew that that was the only way. I mean the Ku Klux Klan was walking around with guns. Look I come up in Klan country so I don’t want nobody telling me nothing about the Klan now. These weren’t no Bible toting — they wanted to talk that Bible toting stuff but you talk about a contradiction. Don’t pass that bullshit to me because I know. I was with my father when I was a kid and my brother and I and we were going through a lot, a used car lot in Indianapolis. And I was about six years old. And you know how little kids are, you get in the car and you’re trying to act like you’re driving. And I’ll never forget this guy looked — to me, as a six year old, he looked like he was about seven feet tall. A white man, he came and pulled me out of the car and said, “You little curly haired Nigger” and kicked me right in the crack of my ass. I felt every bit of that man’s shoe in my ass, and kicked me so hard I pissed on myself. And I’ll never forget that. But I’m not bitter about it. But it just taught me something. I learned a lesson from that. And my father, and the way my father handled the situation taught me a lot about maintaining my cool. Because naturally my father came to my defense. But he didn’t get into no thing where he probably would have been hauled off to jail and this, that and the other. He handled it so diplomatically. And he put the man in his place and let him know that he was totally out of order. Here’s this little kid, what was he doing? He can’t even reach the pedals. He can barely shift the gears. What are you talking about? You know these are the days of the clutch. I’m talking about 1941 Plymouths and stuff like that. This is before dyna-flow and all this other stuff with the automatic gearshifts and all that stuff. No way — what was I going to do with that car? And I wasn’t in there trashing the car or anything like that. But I’ll never forget that and it taught me something. And not just in terms of relationships between black and white people, but there’s good and bad in every ethnic group. It’s just like now I feel bad about the kind of rap that people who are Islamic are getting. That there’s all this racial profiling that’s going on. People have to be very careful about that. And I know everybody’s very uptight. Look I saw, in my apartment in New York in Manhattan I looked out my window, I was up at twenty minutes of nine to answer the telephone and I looked out my window and had a straight shot of the Twin Towers right from my bedroom. It was just like a straight shot from my bedroom window I could see that. I saw that building on fire. I thought it was just a fire. And I said well maybe the sprinklers are going to put it out but I couldn’t believe what was happening. And the next thing I know, bamm. And New York became — Manhattan became an armed camp with the National Guard the state and local police. It was one of the most traumatic things anybody would want to go to who

has never been in a war zone. You were literally in a war zone. I couldn’t even go past a certain point, perimeter, in my neighborhood unless I could produce I.D., a driver’s license that stated I lived in a certain area, they wouldn’t let me go. And I needed to go out of town and I couldn’t even get out of the airport because the flights were all canceled. And I needed to have a pair of pants altered, you know, some cuffs put on my pants, I couldn’t even go to the tailor because the National Guard guys wouldn’t let me go into the block. They said you have no business there, you don’t live there so you can’t go. I said but I’ve got to get my pants fixed man, I’m not a terrorist, I just need to get my pants fixed. The tension and everything that existed in that city, but the way people came together. New York is a beautiful place. Because in spite of the fact that people think New York and people ask me how can you live in New York oh my God. People getting mugged and this, that and the other. But New York has got the best of the best, it’s got the worst of the worst, and all the different — it’s yin and yang and everything in between. And to see how people came together. And people were in tears and it was just a very traumatic experience. I didn’t know what had happened to my youngest brother. He worked for the Social Security department right down in that area. And I was worried about him all day and finally in the afternoon I went out to the post office and I was coming out of the post office which is right across the street from where I live. And I see this guy standing up there and he’s got all this ash and stuff on him, it was my brother.

And he saw me and he was just — like he was in a daze. And when he saw me he just grabbed me. He’s taller than I am and he was just beating me, “Oh Larry, oh man, I’m so glad, do you know man I could have been in that building, it could have been me, we were talking to one of our colleagues who was in the building and we were telling him to get out and the guy was talking about they’ve told us to stay, that just sit tight, he said, and he’s gone now.” You know so I had to take him, I took him up to my apartment. He had walked all the way from the World Trade Center up to where I live at 14th Street and Avenue A. And I took him upstairs and we went and got a six pack of beer, because I had to settle him down. And he took a shower and I gave him a sweat outfit of mine to put on so he’d have some clean clothes. But you see all these kind of things, it’s all related to the music. People might watch this and say well we got off on a tangent.

But it’s a part of what we’re talking about in terms of the human condition, the human existence. And all that’s a part of the music. And when a person gets up to improvise they have to reflect that in their music and that’s a part of who and what you are. And so this whole thing about the jazz education and how commercialized it is in certain instances,
